[The arc]{.kicker}

## Where this sits in the semester

The Object Fair closes the loop. It is the last review of A4, read against the same spine we have used since Week 1.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[A1: Total Recall<br/>Weeks 1-3] --> B[A2: Evidence + Workflow Map<br/>Weeks 4-6]
    B --> C[A3: Prototype + Verification<br/>Weeks 7-9]
    C --> D[A4: Workflow Package<br/>Weeks 10-12]
    D --> E{Final review}
    E --> F[Object Fair: present & defend]
    E --> G[Transfer: reasoning you keep]
```

::: {.concept-card}
One method, four objects. Today you hand over the **package** — and then you keep the **reasoning**.
:::

---

[The session]{.kicker}

## Run of show

A calm, predictable order so no one over-prepares for a slot.

| Segment | Time | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| Setup & final check | 15 min | files loaded, object cards posted, timing confirmed |
| Welcome & framing | 5 min | the evaluation loop we all read against |
| Final presentations | ~90 min | timed, with questions after each |
| Invited critic notes | 20 min | practice and method perspectives |
| Session 2: round table | 30 min | synthesis and transfer forward |

::: {.example-card}
[While others present]{.card-title}
You are not waiting your turn — you are reviewing. Note one strong move and one open question per presenter. Those notes are your participation record.
:::

---

## Presentation format

::: {.activity-card}
[Per person]{.card-title}
- **6–8 min** — final presentation of your A4 package
- **4 min** — questions from the room and invited critics
- **2 min** — notes captured, one carry-forward noted
:::

Use your object card as the single visual that carries the recommendation and the one figure. Volunteers go first; a random draw may fill the remaining slots.

---

[The criteria]{.kicker}

## What every presentation is read against

Each package is read against one evaluation loop — the same logic your A4 must let a stranger trace.

::: {.spine-rail}
[Decision]{.node} [Evidence]{.node} [Variation]{.node} [Output]{.node} [Threshold]{.node} [Action]{.node}
:::

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[design decision] --> B[variants / scenarios]
    B --> C[workflow]
    C --> D[evidence output]
    D --> E{threshold}
    E --> F[design action]
    F --> G[limit]
```

::: {.concept-card}
[The reviewer's question]{.card-title}
Can I trace **decision → variants/scenarios → workflow → evidence output → threshold → action → limit** without you explaining it out loud?
:::

If a link is missing, that is feedback — not a verdict.

---

## Invited critics: three reading positions

Not judges with scores — three perspectives, so the feedback is varied rather than repetitive.

:::: {.three-step}
::: {.step-box}
[Practice lens]{.card-title}
Would this convince a studio tutor or client? Is the recommendation usable?
:::
::: {.step-box}
[Method lens]{.card-title}
Is the workflow sound? Are assumptions, thresholds, and limits stated?
:::
::: {.step-box}
[Communication lens]{.card-title}
Can a busy reader get the message in 30 seconds?
:::
::::

---

## Q&A that helps the presenter

The questions that help most are the ones that test a link in the loop, not the person.

::: {.activity-card}
[Useful questions sound like]{.card-title}
- "What would have changed the recommendation?" (threshold)
- "How would someone rerun this?" (workflow)
- "Where does this stop being true?" (limit)
:::

::: {.warning-card}
We examine the artifact and its claim, never the presenter's competence.
:::

---

## Capture feedback as you go

You will hear more than you can hold. Sort it while it is fresh.

| Note type | Meaning | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| **Trace gap** | a link in the loop is unclear | record it for the final package edit |
| **Carry-forward** | a move worth reusing next time | add to your transfer list |
| **Polish** | small clarity improvement | note if time allows |

::: {.reflection-card}
The skill is not defending everything. It is hearing one true note and knowing what to do with it.
:::

## BREAK {.big-break}

Take 10 minutes.

When you return, we move from presenting to synthesis — what reasoning you keep.

[Session 2 · Round table]{.kicker}

## The reasoning you can transfer

::: {.spine-rail}
[Decision]{.node} [Evidence]{.node} [Variation]{.node} [Output]{.node} [Threshold]{.node} [Action]{.node .is-current}
:::

This is synthesis, not a second formal presentation. Using your final object card or reflection note, speak for 60–90 seconds on the reasoning you would carry into another project. [feeds A4]{.feeds-tag}

Volunteers go first; a random draw may fill the remaining turns.

---

## Reconstruct what transfers

**Object this week: the reasoning you can transfer to another project.**

::: {.recall-4step}
::: {.step}**Did** What was the core reasoning move in your A4 workflow? :::
::: {.step}**Assumed** What did it depend on that was specific to this project? :::
::: {.step}**Risk** Where might that reasoning break on a different problem? :::
::: {.step}**Verify** What would you check before reusing it next time? :::
:::

::: {.grading-note}
Post your four-step under your object card. Posting + an honest reconstruction is the graded unit — not how you spoke. Session 2 today is synthesis; there is no second graded presentation.
:::

---

## Transfer forward

::: {.reflection-card}
[What do you keep?]{.card-title}
Take three minutes and write:

- which reasoning move from A4 will I reuse in studio?
- what evidence habit is now part of how I work?
- where will I still need to slow down and check?
- what is one decision I will treat differently next time?
:::

Keep it in notes or post it as a Slack thread under your object card.

---

[Exit]{.kicker}

## Your transfer line, in one sentence

Before you leave, write and post:

::: {.reflection-card}
**The one reasoning move I am keeping from this course is ___, and the next project I will use it on is ___.**
:::

Thank you for the work, the honesty, and for examining each other's reasoning rather than each other. That habit is the part that travels with you.
